title: A Cat Called Kush: Studies on Harmony and Dialogue Across Media
abstract:
In the fall of 2018, I participated in Northwestern University’s semester-long Art, Literature, and Contemporary European Thought program in Paris, France, in association with two French universities: Sciences Po and Université Sorbonne Nouvelle III. During the program, I was able to conduct research on some of the most significant art works and literary achievements of the 19th, 20th, and 21st centuries. This program inspired a project I completed during the summer of 2019, when I was awarded a Northwestern Summer Undergraduate Research Grant for a practice-based study that explored how the same stories can be told through different media. Over the course of nine weeks, I completed a series of interrelated art works, all relating to the experiences I had while studying in France. I began with notes, sketches, and painted studies of photographs I had taken of the city. From these sketches, I began my first large scale oil painting. During this time, I started writing a short fiction story, a narrative inspired by the notes and the overall process of my first painting. I continued experimenting with this method of production, completing three large oil paintings, a graphite drawing, a book of sketches, a series of short fiction stories, and a sculptural piece by the end of the summer. My project concluded in September 2019, when the pieces were installed in Northwestern’s Kresge Centennial Hall gallery space. The exhibition demonstrated my efforts to harmonize color, image, and the written word. 

My own creative process as a writer and artist is inspired by the coalescence of painting, illustration, and literature. One of the works of art that has motivated my own practice is "Prose on the Trans-Siberian Railway and of Little Jehanne of France" (1913) by Sonia Delaunay. This piece unites both color and text through abstract painting and free verse poetry, and is presented on a tall, vertically orientated sheet of creased parchment with two distinct halves. On the left side, Delaunay’s colorful circles, blotches, and swirls subtly bleed into the right-hand column, which features a poem written by the novelist and poet Blaise Cendrars. While the painting explores how colors interact with one another and the poem tells the story of a voyage by train, both are presented by the artist and the writer as one. Both share themes of movement, a journey shown through story and color. For me, this piece raises an important question: what new form is created when existing media are combined? Similarly, the surrealist novel "Nadja," by André Breton, has inspired my own artistic studies. His striking use of photographs, sketches, and portraiture within the textual narrative of the story seem to blur the boundaries between reality and fiction, something that I am exploring in my creative work today. I am drawn to the locations where media intersect, and the interdisciplinary forms that are produced within that space.
